Keywords: Surprise Attack on New Carthage and Scipio's Wading Assault
Scipio's continence and the returned bride
RagShortTexts: In 209 BC the 24-year-old Scipio, having gauged the depth of the lagoon at ebb tide, waded across to take New Carthage by surprise, and won the hearts of the Spanish tribes with his generosity and clemency.

Variants.Content: In 209 BC Publius Cornelius Scipio (later known as Scipio Africanus), only twenty-four years old, took up command in Spain as proconsul at a moment of crisis and changed the course of the war with an astonishing strategic surprise. Bypassing the three Carthaginian armies scattered across the Iberian interior, he struck like lightning at New Carthage (Cartagena), Carthage's nerve center and main supply depot in Europe. From local fishermen Scipio learned that the shallow lagoon on the north side dropped sharply in the afternoon under the ebb and the sea wind. So while a frontal assault drew the defenders' attention, he personally led five hundred picked men with scaling ladders on foot through the knee-deep lagoon, and climbed the lightly defended northern wall by surprise to take the city. In this one stroke Rome captured the silver war chest Carthage had accumulated over decades, its shipyards, a huge store of siege catapults, and more than three hundred Iberian noble hostages. Presented with a beautiful Celtiberian bride among the hostages, Scipio not only left her untouched but returned her unharmed to her betrothed, Allucius, and gave back the large ransom as a wedding gift. This incomparable gentlemanly clemency and great strategic talent drove powerful tribal chiefs such as Indibilis and Mandonius over to Rome, shattering the foundations of Barcid rule on the peninsula.

In the hearts of Roman citizens, the fall of New Carthage was a miracle that Neptune, god of the sea, revealed to Scipio in person in a dream! After his father and uncle had died in blood in Spain, the young Scipio not only washed away the bitter disgrace of the house of the Cornelii but also conquered the wild tribes of Spain with the highest aristocratic virtue of old Rome (Clementia). Faced with countless gold and silver he was not greedy; faced with a peerless beauty he was not lustful, and he raised the civilized good faith of the Romans to a height that drew the admiration of the gods. From this battle on, the Roman legions not only won back Spain but also proclaimed to the whole Mediterranean: a new god of war of Rome has come!

The loss of New Carthage was the deadliest disaster Carthage suffered in the Second Punic War. Because the three Carthaginian commanders, Hasdrubal Barca, Mago and Hasdrubal Gisco, distrusted one another and divided their forces too widely, this capital fortress, which held the treasury of the whole European empire, all the reserves of military pay, the finest workshops and the most important tribal hostages, was cleverly taken in only a few days by the young Scipio wading through the water. The loss of New Carthage not only caused the Iberian tribes to defect and rebel swiftly, but also completely cut the sea routes and silver supply that Hannibal urgently needed in Italy, reducing Carthage's more than ten years of glorious expansion in Europe to nothing.
